# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure for Stroke Prevention in Atrial Fibrillation: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and rationale

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained arrhythmia, and its incidence and prevalence are increasing in the United States and globally. [1] Oral anticoagulation (OAC) remains the cornerstone of thromboembolic prophylaxis, yet a substantial proportion of eligible patients are undertreated owing to bleeding risk and intolerance, and warfarin carries an inherent hazard of intracranial hemorrhage. The conceptual basis for percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) rests on the observation, drawn from pathological, surgical, and echocardiographic studies, that in contrast to patients with valvular AF, the left atrial appendage (LAA) may be the major source for emboli in nonvalvular AF, based on an analysis of 23 studies utilizing echocardiographic, operative, and postmortem evaluations. [2] Mechanical exclusion of the LAA therefore offers a site-specific, non-pharmacological alternative to lifelong anticoagulation. [3]

## Pivotal randomized trials versus warfarin

The first randomized evidence came from PROTECT AF. This multicenter study determined whether percutaneous LAA closure with a filter device (Watchman) was noninferior to warfarin for stroke prevention; 707 patients with nonvalvular AF and at least one risk factor were randomized to the Watchman device (n=463) or continued warfarin (n=244) in a 2:1 ratio, with warfarin continued for about 45 days after implantation, followed by clopidogrel for 4.5 months and lifelong aspirin. [4] Closure met noninferiority criteria for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death, but an early safety hazard—principally pericardial effusion—was identified. [4] Longer-term follow-up subsequently demonstrated superiority over warfarin for the primary composite endpoint and reduced cardiovascular and all-cause mortality. Reddy and colleagues reported these results in JAMA in 2014 (312:1988–1998). [5]

The confirmatory PREVAIL trial was designed to address the safety concerns. It assessed LAA occlusion in patients with a CHADS2 score ≥2, or 1 plus another risk factor, again comparing the Watchman device with long-term warfarin therapy. [6] At 18 months the first coprimary efficacy endpoint did not achieve the prespecified noninferiority criterion, whereas the second coprimary endpoint (stroke or systemic embolism beyond 7 days) did achieve noninferiority, and early safety events occurred in only 2.2% of the Watchman arm, significantly lower than in PROTECT AF. [6] A patient-level analysis of both trials at five years confirmed comparable composite outcomes with reductions in hemorrhagic stroke and mortality. These 5-year outcomes were published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology (2017;70:2964–2975). [7]

## Anticoagulation-ineligible patients

Because PROTECT AF mandated transient warfarin, the ASAP study tested closure without anticoagulation. This multicenter prospective study enrolled 150 patients with nonvalvular AF and CHADS2 ≥1 considered ineligible for warfarin, with a primary endpoint combining ischemic stroke, hemorrhagic stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular/unexplained death. [8] Observed ischemic stroke rates were markedly lower than expected with antiplatelet therapy alone, supporting feasibility in this challenging group. [8]

## Comparisons with direct oral anticoagulants

As DOACs became standard, the PRAGUE-17 trial provided the first head-to-head randomized comparison. This multicenter noninferiority trial compared LAAC with DOACs in patients with nonvalvular AF who had a history of bleeding, a cardioembolic event on OAC, and/or a CHA2DS2-VASc ≥3 and HAS-BLED >2. [9] Among these high-risk patients, LAAC was noninferior to DOAC in preventing major AF-related cardiovascular, neurological, and bleeding events. [9] In long-term follow-up, LAAC remained noninferior to DOACs and nonprocedural bleeding was significantly reduced with LAAC. [10]

The OPTION trial extended this question to patients undergoing AF ablation. This prospective randomized multicenter trial compared LAAC with OAC in more than 1,500 patients with elevated stroke risk after catheter ablation, and demonstrated that LAAC was noninferior to OAC for the composite of all-cause death, stroke, or systemic embolization and superior for non–procedure-related bleeding. [11] At 36 months, a primary safety endpoint event had occurred in 8.5% of the LAAC group versus 18.1% of the anticoagulation group. [11]

## Device evolution and comparative performance

Iterative device design has improved outcomes. The next-generation Watchman FLX was evaluated in PINNACLE FLX. The primary safety endpoint was met with a low adverse event rate of 0.5%, the primary effectiveness endpoint was met with a 100% rate of effective LAA closure at 12 months, and the implant success rate was 98.8%. [12] Real-world registry data have corroborated this performance; in the NCDR LAAO Registry, among 97,185 patients undergoing Watchman FLX, successful implantation occurred in 97.5% and the key safety endpoint occurred in 0.45%. [13]

The Amulet IDE trial provided the first large randomized comparison of two devices. The dual-seal Amulet occluder was noninferior for safety and effectiveness of stroke prevention compared with the Watchman device and superior for LAA occlusion, although procedure-related complications were higher with Amulet and decreased with operator experience. [14]

## Procedural complications and residual leak

Two device-specific complications warrant vigilance. Device-related thrombus (DRT) may form on the atrial face of the implant. Thrombus may form on the left atrial face of the device and then potentially embolize; Dukkipati and colleagues studied its incidence, predictors, and clinical outcomes in a large series of Watchman cohorts. [15] Peri-device leak is also common; an NCDR analysis suggested that small leaks (<5 mm) may be clinically relevant as they were associated with a small but statistically significant increase in ischemic events. [16] Achieving a complete seal is challenging because the size, shape, and orientation of the LAA are widely variable, so achieving complete occlusion using fixed-shape devices has proven difficult. [16]

## Guidelines and future directions

Contemporary practice is shaped by the 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation, which incorporates LAAC for selected patients at elevated stroke risk, particularly those with contraindications to long-term anticoagulation. [17] With randomized evidence now spanning warfarin, antiplatelet-only regimens, and DOACs, LAAC has matured from an experimental procedure into an established therapeutic option. Ongoing priorities include defining the optimal post-implant antithrombotic regimen, minimizing DRT and peri-device leak, and clarifying the role of concomitant closure during AF ablation. [11][14]
